result.summary: The text surveys the many cities and parents claimed for Homer and Hesiod, quotes the Pythia's oracles about Homer's origin, and gives a genealogy linking both poets to Apollo and Orpheus. It then begins the story of their contest at Chalcis, where Hesiod questions Homer.

scenes.title: Rival claims to Homer's origin
scenes.summary: The writer lists the cities and parents claimed for Homer and the poets' native places, and the sources of the name Homer.

scenes.title: Pythia answers Emperor Hadrian
scenes.summary: The Pythia tells Hadrian in verse that Homer was from Ithaca, son of Telemachus and Epicasta.

scenes.title: Genealogy of the poets
scenes.summary: A line of descent from Apollo is traced to Hesiod and Homer.

scenes.title: Homer consults the Pythia
scenes.summary: Homer, after the Margites, asks at Delphi who he is and is warned of Ios and a riddle.
scenes.stakes: Homer's death on Ios and the riddle of the young children.

scenes.title: The contest at Chalcis begins
scenes.summary: At Amphidamas' funeral games, Hesiod questions Homer before the judges.
scenes.stakes: The poets' reputation and the judges' prize.

alias_notes.explanation: Name Smyrnaeans said Homer bore, 'born of Meles', before he went blind.

notable_quotes.reason: Homer's famous pessimistic answer: best never to be born, otherwise to die quickly.
Hesiod's bitter description of his home village Ascra.

analysis.text: The passage shows how Greeks competed over the origins of their great poets, giving them divine ancestry and rival birthplaces.
Including a Hadrian-era oracle shows the text was compiled in the 2nd century AD, long after the poets lived.

legacy.text: Homer's answer that it is best never to be born echoes a traditional Greek pessimistic saying also found in Theognis and Sophocles.

fun_facts.text: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod draws on an earlier version by the sophist Alcidamas, and Nietzsche wrote about it.

language_notes.text: The syntax is awkward: 'his particular countrymen' means each city claims both poets, or each claims Homer, as its own native son.
'Epithet' here means a descriptive name; the writer says 'homeros' was Smyrnaean usage for blind people, hence the poet's later name.
Homeridae means 'sons of Homer', a guild or family of rhapsodes on Chios who recited and preserved his poems.
The Margites was a comic mock-epic about a fool, anciently attributed to Homer but now thought not to be his.
Telemachus is Odysseus' son in the Odyssey; making him Homer's father would tie the poet to his own epic's family. This translation otherwise uses Ulysses elsewhere, but here says Odysseus.
The Ithacan slave-woman story echoes the Odyssey's world of Ithaca and Phoenician traders; Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry.
Aeolians were Greek settlers on the northwest coast of Asia Minor; the writer says their dialect used 'homeros' for blind.
"Siren" here is a figurative term for a sweet-voiced singer, not the sea-monster; "heavenly" marks Homer's divinely gifted song.
"The mother that bare him" uses archaic "bare" for "bore"; "by far the wisest of mortal kind" is an oracular superlative.
The grandfather is Nestor, whom Homer glorifies in the Iliad and Odyssey, as the wise old king of Pylos.
The Margites is a comic mock-epic about a foolish man, anciently attributed to Homer but now lost apart from fragments.
The riddle of the young children refers to the legend that Homer died on Ios from failing to solve a riddle posed by fisher boys.
"Gates of Hades" means the entrance to the underworld, so the line says it is best to die as soon as possible after birth.

context_notes.text: Hesiod's quoted lines come from his Works and Days, where he describes his father's move from Aeolian Cyme to Ascra in Boeotia.
Smyrna was an Ionian city on the coast of Asia Minor; the Meles was a river there, and Melesigenes means 'born of Meles'.
These names are ancient scholars and writers who offered competing genealogies; the passage shows how little reliable evidence existed about Homer's life.
Hadrian was Roman emperor (reigned 117-138 AD) and a keen philhellene; the anecdote shows later interest in Homer's birthplace.
The Pythia was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi, whose oracles were traditionally given in hexameter verse.
Funeral games, athletic and other contests held in honor of a dead man, were a Greek custom; Hesiod mentions this very contest in Works and Days.
Chalcis was a principal city of Euboea, an island off the eastern coast of mainland Greece.

literary_notes.text: Hesiod's own bitter description lends first-person authority and contrasts with the vagueness about Homer, who never names himself.
Cities are treated as mothers claiming a son, dramatizing civic pride and rivalry over the poet.
The rapid list of names and authorities mimics epic cataloguing and stresses how confused and contradictory the tradition is.
Calling Homer a "siren" figures his enchanting song as irresistible, borrowing the Sirens' seductive voices.
The oracle's warning about Ios and the riddle anticipates Homer's death, shaping the legend's tragic close.
Homer's grim answer about never being born contrasts with the festive setting and with his own celebrated life of song.
